raw_case_text:
A 25-year-old woman was admitted to our emergency department with a subacute onset of mild confusion and left hemiparesis (Medical Research Council grade 4/5). She was fully alert and orientated, complaining about headaches (Visual Analogic Scale 7/10). She had no history of drug abuse or cigarette smoking.
Pre- and postcontrast computed tomography (CT) scans of the brain [Figure 1] revealed a 2 cm diameter hypodense nodular lesion in the right thalamus with perilesional edema causing moderate mass effect, with colliquative features inside. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) pre and post contrast [Figure 2] confirmed a right thalamic nodular lesion measuring 25 x 22 mm, with perilesional edema. The nodule appeared hypointense on T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences, isointense on T1-weighted and reg-diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) sequences. The nodule and associated edema resulted in ipsilateral ventricular compression. In the coronal sections [Figure 3], there was an irregular postcontrast enhancement, especially along the nodule walls. Was also visible an inner enhancing nodule, which should have raised the suspicion of parasitic infection [Figure 3, Panel C].
The clinical presentation (without any known history of immune suppression) and the neuroimaging features of the solitary brain lesion primarily suggested a brain tumor, even if other diagnostic hypotheses could not be rejected.
Considering the deep location in an eloquent area, it was decided to perform a neuronavigated stereotaxic biopsy [Figure 4]. Preoperative planning was conducted using three-dimensional reconstruction to simulate the surgical trajectory and avoid functional areas and tracts (StealthStation S8; Medtronic, Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA) [Figure 4].
A coronal trajectory was used passing lateral to the lateral ventricle wall. Histopathology revealed extensive areas of necrosis, vascular thrombosis phenomena and aspects of vasculitis with lymphohistiocytic and granulocytic infiltrate at the level of the vascular walls. Rounded structures containing eosinophilic corpuscles inside the infiltrate were found, suggesting a protozoal infection, and allowing the diagnosis of cerebral toxoplasmosis [Figure 5].
The immediate postoperative course was uneventful without complications. Nevertheless, in the following days, the patient presented with fever and abdominal pain with rapid clinical worsening and septic shock. Therefore, the patient was then transferred to intensive care unit. A total-body CT scan revealed multiple abscesses (liver, kidney, and thyroid gland), intestinal walls thickening, and pleural effusion [Figure 6].
Due to the septic shock and the diagnosis of toxoplasmosis, the patient was evaluated by the infectious disease specialist, who initiated the treatment of toxoplasmosis and performed a serologic test which revealed an HIV infection.
Despite therapy, due to HIV-related immunosuppression, the patient suffered multiorgan failure and died.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a subacute onset of mild confusion, left hemiparesis, and severe headache.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed subacute mild confusion accompanied by left-sided weakness and headache rated 7/10 on the Visual Analog Scale prior to admission, with no known prior history of immunosuppression.
subjective.past_medical_history: No known past medical history of immunosuppression. Negative history of cigarette smoking or illicit drug abuse.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for headache (VAS 7/10) and left-sided weakness.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, the patient was alert and oriented with mild confusion and left hemiparesis (Medical Research Council grade 4/5).
objective.advanced_workup: Pre- and post-contrast brain CT revealed a 2 cm hypodense nodular lesion in the right thalamus with colliquative internal features and perilesional edema causing moderate mass effect. Pre- and post-contrast brain MRI confirmed a 25 x 22 mm right thalamic nodular lesion appearing hypointense on T2/FLAIR and isointense on T1/DWI, with irregular peripheral ring enhancement, an inner eccentric enhancing nodule, perilesional edema, and ipsilateral lateral ventricular compression. Neuronavigated stereotactic biopsy (StealthStation S8) of the right thalamic lesion demonstrated extensive necrosis, vascular thrombosis, vasculitis with lymphohistiocytic and granulocytic infiltration of vessel walls, and rounded structures containing eosinophilic corpuscles diagnostic of protozoal infection. Following subsequent postoperative deterioration with fever, abdominal pain, and septic shock, a total-body CT scan revealed multiple abscesses in the liver, kidney, and thyroid gland, intestinal wall thickening, and pleural effusion.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Disseminated and cerebral toxoplasmosis unmasking previously undiagnosed HIV infection, complicated by septic shock and multiorgan failure. Initial neuroimaging differential of solitary primary brain tumor was ruled out by stereotactic brain biopsy histopathology confirming Toxoplasma gondii protozoal corpuscles, and subsequent infectious disease evaluation with HIV serology confirmed underlying HIV infection. Despite targeted anti-toxoplasmosis therapy and intensive care unit support, the patient progressed to refractory septic shock and multiorgan failure secondary to severe HIV-related immunosuppression and died.
